POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 06 Nov 2026 11:07:34 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Ursula von der Leyen to visit Black Sea amid wave of deadly drone attacks https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-von-der-leyen-to-visit-black-sea-amid-wave-of-deadly-drone-attacks/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 11:05:01 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9285465 BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is slated to visit Bulgaria and Romania next week, following a series of drone attacks on Black Sea vessels that have heightened security tensions along NATO’s eastern flank.

According to three European Commission officials familiar with the plans, von der Leyen is expected to travel to both countries after attending the COP climate summit in Turkey. “It’s now the deadliest shipping route in the world,” said one of the officials, who was granted anonymity to speak about security-related plans.

At least seven commercial vessels were reportedly struck by drones in the Black Sea last month, leaving two sailors dead and at least 25 missing. The attacks, which Romania blames on Russia, have brought the violence of the war in Ukraine dangerously close to NATO territory.

Romania has warned that the strikes are part of Moscow’s escalating aggression against Ukraine, while Bulgaria has stopped short of formally blaming Moscow, referring instead to drones coming from “an eastern direction.”

The security concerns reached Bulgaria’s shores Friday, when a local resident discovered a drone washed up near the coastal town of Shabla. The aerial vehicle appeared to have been carried ashore by the sea, said the municipality’s mayor, Mariyan Zhechev. The drone’s origin and whether it was connected to the recent attacks on commercial shipping have not been established.

Details of von der Leyen’s itinerary remain scarce, with some European commissioners’ offices unaware of the planned trip. It is also unclear whether she will be accompanied by anyone else such as European Council President António Costa or EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.

The plans come as NATO allies step up surveillance over the Black Sea following the attacks on commercial shipping. Italian, British and American reconnaissance aircraft were spotted conducting simultaneous missions over the region Tuesday, according to Bulgarian broadcaster bTV, while France has extended the deployment of a maritime patrol aircraft in Romania.

The deteriorating security situation is also prompting diplomatic efforts to protect commercial shipping. Speaking at Saturday’s G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said India and Turkey had put forward proposals to help grain-carrying vessels navigate the Black Sea safely amid the continuing Russia-Ukraine war.

]]> en Trump teases ‘beautiful’ deal covering ‘all of Europe’ after meeting Putin’s envoy https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-trump-europe-ukraine-deal-vladimir-putin-envoy-kirill-dmitriev/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:04:57 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9284967 U.S. President Donald Trump reiterated his promise of a “big, beautiful agreement” on Ukraine after holding a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Thursday.

]]> en ‘I don’t trust them’: Lithuanian president warns Putin’s provocations will continue https://www.politico.eu/article/lithuania-president-gitanas-nauseda-vladimir-putin-provocation/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 08:03:08 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9281892 Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda doesn’t think a conventional Russian attack on NATO territory is likely for now, but expects Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s provocations to continue.

The hybrid war will therefore continue, not only on NATO’s eastern flank but also in Germany, Denmark and other countries, Nausėda explained. Russia is testing “how determined we are and whether we will respond collectively when certain red lines are crossed,” the Lithuanian president said.

Putin will make demands that are unacceptable to Ukraine from the outset, he added. “If Ukraine gets through this winter, and I am convinced that it will, the chances of serious talks will improve in 2027. I don’t expect them any earlier.”

]]> en How to curry favor with the next US president — without annoying Trump https://www.politico.eu/article/how-to-curry-favor-with-the-next-us-president-without-annoying-trump/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9279459 LONDON — Donald Trump is badly bruised after this week’s U.S. midterm elections trouncing — but Britain’s diplomatic corps needs to avoid looking like it’s going all-in on the jubilant Democrats.

That’s the advice of Ed Roman, the former director of communications at the British Embassy in Washington. He spent five years on the embassy’s senior leadership team, serving during the Biden and second Trump administrations. It gave him a front row seat as diplomats adjusted to a radical change in U.S. political direction — a task they now face again.

In his first podcast interview since leaving the civil service a month ago, Roman tells POLITICO’s Westminster Insider that British diplomats need to show they can cultivate sophisticated ties with Trump’s possible successors — without provoking the ire of the current White House incumbent. Here are his top tips.

1) Don’t be late to the party

“If you’re doing it now, you’re kind of too late,” Roman says of efforts to schmooze key Democrats who have made it into both the Senate and House this week. The British Embassy has, he says, already been doing its homework, tracking potential Democratic Party contenders throughout the year in anticipation of a wave.

But there’s stiff global competition to build those links first. “The French competitors, the German competitors, the Korean competitors — each embassy is trying to build a network that allows them a level of access,” he says.

In addition to the embassy in D.C., Britain uses its eight U.S. consulates — strategically placed across the country — to help it identify rising politicians outside Washington.

As Roman puts it: “Real politics in America happens in America, out in the states, out in the districts. Knowing those Senate hopefuls ahead of time is always the name of the game.”

2) Don’t put all your eggs in one basket

Roman worked under former British Ambassador Karen Pierce, whose team invested considerable effort in cultivating relationships with Trump’s circle during the Biden administration.

Roman believes that work paid “dividends” for Britain in the years that followed, including in landing a U.K.-U.S. trade deal as Trump slapped tariffs on a host of allies.

But he cautions that the next president might not seem as obvious as Trump — who has had an iron grip on his party for years — did back then. “It’s a complete surprise that you always need to watch [out] for,” Roman notes.

It’s vital to build diplomatic relationships with a broad field — including other presidential hopefuls and figures who might end up in a future Cabinet, White House or national security team.

“Yes, you’re looking to identify the front runner, but you’re also looking to get to know the people around them. And very often they’re the people that are useful to you as an embassy,” he says.

3) Hold your ground — but don’t show off

It’s important not to provoke Trump’s ire by making him feel British diplomacy is already moving on. But Roman argues that embassies must also be prepared to defend their right to engage opposition politicians.

“This is perfectly legitimate business, there’s nothing nefarious about this,” he says.

He points to Trump officials openly engaging with British politicians across party lines.

“That is legitimate diplomatic business and there’s a bit of pushback that you sometimes have to do with administrations to be upfront about that,” he says.

There is, however, a big difference between quietly cultivating a future president and publicly advertising the fact.

Roman warns against the temptation to “grandstand a little bit that you’ve just had this brilliant session with [Gavin] Newsom [the Democratic governor of California] or whoever” on social media after meeting a potential successor. “That stuff does irritate the presidency,” he adds.

“Doing it in a discreet way, focusing on the interpersonal rather than the comms bounce that you might get out of it back in London is really key,” he advises.

4) Always big up Britain 

Simply getting a meeting with a rising Democrat isn’t enough. British diplomats need to convince prospective presidents that a strong relationship with Britain will actually be useful to them.

He warns that the next generation of American leaders may have fewer historic connections to Britain, meaning the U.K. cannot assume its traditional “special relationship” status will automatically open doors.

“For each generation politically, you’ve always got to, in effect, restate your offer,” he says.

Roman tells the podcast: “You can’t just tip up and say, you know: Hi, I’m John or James or Karen from the British Embassy, let’s have a chat.

“You’ve really got to dig into what their campaign is about, how are we useful to them? What do they understand about Britain? What do they know about Britain? What is Britain’s offer to them if they are successful and they come into power?”

5) Never assume a return to “normal”

Even if Democrats win the White House in 2028, Roman cautions British diplomats not to assume cultivating ties will automatically produce an easier relationship than it has with Trump.

Each country has its own blunt interests, and Roman recalls that the Biden administration was not an uncomplicated partner for Britain.

“There’s a bit of amnesia going on in the sense that the Biden administration were very challenging to deal with,” he says. “They were not particularly sentimental about Britain.”

And he argues that this week’s midterm results should not be mistaken for a wholesale rejection of Trump’s “America First” worldview.

“It wasn’t an embrace of America as a global policeman,” he says. “It wasn’t an embrace of America’s traditional role presiding over the rules-based international order.”

Economic nationalism and skepticism about America’s global responsibilities could survive Trump, Roman believes — including under a Democratic successor. “We would be, I think, ill-advised to draw the conclusion that any form of normalcy will return,” he says.

Ed Roman was speaking to the Westminster Insider podcast. Listen here.

]]> en From Madrid to MAGA: How Spain’s Vox forged a right-wing network with global reach https://www.politico.eu/article/from-madrid-to-maga-how-spains-vox-forged-a-right-wing-network-with-global-reach/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9254466

From Madrid to MAGA: How Spain’s Vox forged a right-wing network with global reach

The Spanish party has forged strong links among far-right groups stretching from Buenos Aires to Washington — and is wielding growing influence in Brussels.

By AITOR HERNÁNDEZ-MORALES
in Madrid

Photo-illustration by Ben Tallon for POLITICO

With Hungary’s Viktor Orbán gone, Spain’s nationalist Vox party is set to play an increasingly central role as a bridge linking Europe’s far right to political allies worldwide — from South America to MAGA in Washington.

Unlike Orbán’s Fidesz or Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, which have spent decades shaping national and European politics, Vox is a relative newcomer, having only entered Spain’s parliament in 2019.

But it is a force on the march. Pollsters expect Vox to double its parliamentary representation in Spain’s upcoming Nov. 29 election, potentially making it an indispensable partner in a coalition government led by conservative People’s Party chief Alberto Núñez Feijóo.

Advertisement

If the polls hold true, Vox would then arrive in government with an outsized global influence relative to its domestic footprint — all thanks to an international network it has quietly cultivated over the past few years.

Through its Madrid-based Disenso Foundation, the party has established ties with Latin American leaders such as Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast, while forging relationships with influential figures in the MAGA movement in Washington.

Though distinct, the movements are bound by a common rejection of the political establishment. “This isn’t about occupying more space. This is a movement,” Jorge Martín Frías, a Vox member of the European Parliament and director of the Disenso Foundation, told POLITICO in Madrid. Vox’s allies, the lawmaker said, “face the same obstacles, the same labels, the same desire to annihilate them … And that’s how a sense of brotherhood develops.”

That same spirit of cooperation has helped Vox establish itself as a trusted partner to Europe’s right. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, now heads Patriots.eu, the pan-European political group that brings together Fidesz and the National Rally, as well as other far-right parties like Italy’s Lega, Belgium’s Vlaams Belang and Portugal’s Chega.

Frank Furedi, president of the Brussels-based Freedom & Sovereignty Initiative Europe, a conservative think tank formed by the core team behind MCC Brussels, said Vox had “been remarkably effective in carving out a niche for themselves as a movement that’s open to other political forces.”

Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University, said Vox’s strategy had allowed it to amass international influence well beyond what its electoral strength would suggest.

Advertisement

“Vox is an electorally modest party in the European context of the far right,” he said. “But it’s nonetheless become a communications node, a bridge, a hinge between the new Latin American right, the European far right and the Trumpist right.”

Across the Atlantic

Vox has been vocal about its interest in Ibero-America, which comprises Spain, Portugal and the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries of the Americas.

The “continent of hope,” Martín Frías says, is “already ahead of Europe, including in economic terms,” pointing to Milei’s chainsaw approach to deregulation in Argentina and Kast’s efforts to attract foreign investment in Chile through tax incentives and regulatory changes.

Right-wing leaders on the continent “are showing that it is possible to challenge the politics of resignation that have prevailed here — the status quo of the People’s Party and the Socialists,” he added.

Through the Disenso Foundation, created in 2020, the party has built an institutional network of conferences, political contacts and training programs. One of its main initiatives, Foro Madrid, brings together right-wing parties, politicians and organizations from across Latin America.

Vox has funneled millions of euros into Disenso over the last six years, giving it substantial resources to nurture its relationships across the pond.

According to political scientist Fernández Vázquez, Vox identified and reached out to figures like Milei and Kast when their respective movements were still relatively small. Those early contacts have since developed into relationships with leaders who now hold power or occupy prominent positions in their countries.

The network has also given Abascal direct access to some of the region’s most prominent political figures, such as Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. During an April visit to Madrid, she met with the Vox leader while notably declining an offer to meet Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Advertisement

Martín Frías attributed Vox’s success in building an international network to its refusal to simply export a Spanish political model and its ability not to get caught up in disagreements over national interests.

He pointed to Argentina’s support for the EU-Mercosur trade deal, which Vox opposes. “Each country, and each leader, applies its own rules to defend its national interests, which in some cases will be contrary to ours,” he said. “That’s only logical … That’s the game we’re all playing.”

For Vox, Latin America is part of a wider network that includes Washington. Indeed, Martín Frías has taken the party’s message directly to the American conservative establishment, attending the Conservative Political Action Conference in Washington in 2024 alongside Abascal and speaking at events organized by the right-wing think tank The Heritage Foundation, including the 2026 Miami Security Forum.

Furedi said Vox’s most prominent members have displayed a level of interest in Latin America rarely found among their European far-right counterparts. The party, he argued, was interested not just in building political alliances but in fostering “a more dynamic contemporary Hispanic culture.”

Balázs Orbán, Viktor Orbán’s former political director and a senior figure in Hungary’s MCC, told POLITICO that Vox had been able to forge a transatlantic “connection” through the party’s “sophisticated” approach and its members’ ability to speak both English and Spanish.

Back to Brussels

Vox’s approach to language and identity has undoubtedly given it an edge in Brussels.

The party has taken note of others’ mistakes, including those of Le Pen’s National Rally, whose failure to build strong ties with the wider far right has been partly attributed to its members’ refusal to engage in languages other than French.

“[The National Rally] may speak English, but they refuse to speak English … With Vox, there isn’t this desire to speak Spanish and make a big deal out of the fact that they’re very proud of their language. They’re much more relaxed about it,” Furedi said.

Advertisement

Fernández Vázquez said this had helped Vox position itself as a broker in Europe and led other far-right figures to view Abascal as a safe choice to lead Patriots, capable of balancing Le Pen and Orbán’s rival ambitions.

With Orbán’s fall, many are now competing for the influence he once wielded.

“Fidesz obviously wants to maintain its relevance and authority,” Furedi said. “The Italians — [Brothers of Italy] in particular — are also quite keen, with Meloni wanting to be seen as the equivalent of what Orbán was at a certain point.” But Vox stands out due to its consolidated role as both an “honest broker” and global interlocutor, he added.

Vox’s Martín Frías rejected the suggestion that his group was simply waiting to inherit Fidesz’s mantle. Instead, he said, the goal was to unite like-minded parties against institutions such as the European Commission, which he accused of undermining the European Union — a political project which he described as “a good invention.”

The National Rally’s Jordan Bardella similarly said earlier this year his party would not seek to leave the EU, but instead transform it from within and “change everything without destroying anything.”

Like Martín Frías, Balázs Orbán rejected the notion of a far-right handover and referred to the beginnings of a broader alliance, including Hungary’s former prime minister and his party.

“Viktor Orbán always played a very important role in the patriotic movement. He is the founding father and one of its intellectual leading figures,” he said, adding that now that Fidesz is “no longer in government, we have more time to spend in Brussels and speed things up.”

Martín Frías expressed optimism for what Spain’s upcoming election would mean for Vox’s broader mission in Europe.

Advertisement

“Changes of government in European countries can lead to changes in the European Council,” he said, outlining a vision of an EU made up of sovereign nations that pursue their own interests while cooperating where their goals align. “There is an opportunity there to correct everything that is wrong, and to even regain citizens’ trust in the institutions.”

That shift, he argued, is already visible in the European Parliament, where the center-right European People’s Party increasingly “has no choice” but to work with the Patriots.

“They don’t do it out of principle,” Martín Frías said. “They do it because they’re afraid of the electorate.”

]]> en Don’t try to ‘please the dictator,’ Estonian leader urges Europe about Putin https://www.politico.eu/article/estonia-prime-minister-kristen-michal-europe-vladimir-putin-russia/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 06 Nov 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9274809 TALLINN — Europe shouldn’t open a diplomatic channel to Russian President Vladimir Putin, warned the leader of one of the continent’s most exposed nations.

“Europe should not be in a mediator’s position,” Estonia’s Prime Minister Kristen Michal told POLITICO in an interview this week. “You should not take the role of trying to please the dictator.”

European leaders have long feared the U.S. administration under President Donald Trump may pursue a Russia–Ukraine peace deal on terms that sideline Europe and disadvantage Kyiv. The most recent talks between Washington and Moscow have reignited debate in Brussels and national capitals about the need for Europe to have its own direct line to the Kremlin. Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a 90-minute call with Putin in late October.

The Estonian premier — whose country of 1.3 million people borders Russia and has been subject to Moscow’s persistent attempts to stoke internal unrest — warned against the idea of direct talks, saying it would weaken Europe’s position with Putin.

“For once, Europe has a plan which is actually working” by suffocating Russia economically with sanctions, Michal said. Being a mediator means “you are willing to lower the standards, for example, for Russia,” including when it comes to imposing and enforcing punitive sanctions, he said.

“You cannot [have] two roles. One role is backing up Ukraine and pressuring Russia. A second one is trying to have a form of mediation,” the Estonian leader said.

“Putin should understand that Europe is strong, keeping together and we have one voice,” he added.

U.S. officials will sit down with Ukrainian and Russian representatives next week. The talks, which will be the first face-to-face negotiations since February, will be held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said Monday.

The Estonian leader said Europeans “appreciate” the Trump administration’s attempts to broker a peace deal, “but the pressure should be very much on Russia,” he said. “The problem [is] sitting in [the] Kremlin. Nowhere else.”

With Trump’s Republican Party in crisis after a major loss in the U.S. midterm elections Tuesday, Europe is closely watching how the shift of power in the U.S. Congress will influence the president’s position on Ukraine.

“Elections have consequence. So this is a good thing in democracy, that you have checks and balances,” Michal said about the election outcome.

He added the electoral shift could move Washington further “to the better side, more value-based side. And when [the] U.S. is more value-based … that probably is a good message to Ukraine and to Europe.”

To heap pressure on Russia, Estonia has spearheaded a push — together with Poland and Sweden — to toughen up visa rules for Russians, including former fighters who fought on the battlefields in Ukraine. Tallinn has proposed an outright ban on allowing ex-soldiers from Russia’s armed forces access to the EU at large.

Officials believe the tourist visas allow Russian operatives easy access into the bloc to conduct so-called hybrid warfare campaigns — from flying drones over sensitive security sites to sabotage of infrastructure.

EU officials told POLITICO last month the European Commission is planning to put forward proposals in the new year.

Michal said Europe had no time to waste as hybrid attacks keep disrupting services. “You should not have these kind of people running around Europe. So limit the visas,” he said.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:41:38 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Listen: The mental health toll of Europe’s migration policies https://euobserver.com/247374/listen-the-mental-health-toll-of-europes-migration-policies/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:38:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247374 Racism, violence, institutional abandonment and unbearable living conditions.  These are all factors that damage the mental health of migrants and exiled people. That’s exactly what migrants in Ceuta are experiencing since July.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

Racism, violence, institutional abandonment and unbearable living conditions.  These are all factors that damage the mental health of migrants and exiled people. That’s exactly what migrants in Ceuta are experiencing since July. 

Does the EU really care about migrants’ mental health? The conditions in which they often find themselves in Europe create stress, anxiety and a lack of hope. These have very concrete effects on their psychological state.

Léa has been working in Ceuta since July as a volunteer for the non profit organisation No Name Kitchen, that supports migrants and refugees. In an interview with our partner inside the Sphera network, El Salto, she speaks about the migrants she has met so far. Her name has been changed:

“In these months I have seen the change in the boys’ faces. As the weeks passed they transformed. It was them, but it wasn’t them anymore.”

Read more

Afghan pushback survivor fights ‘impossible’ evidence rules in European courts with new UN case against Greece

When journalist Sarah Babiker from El Salto spoke to those who are closest to the migrants in Ceuta, she noticed that they all describe a climate of intense tension and speak about a mental health crisis.

Léa is observing systematic violence on the city streets: “I didn’t find a single person who hadn’t had experiences of violence or racism with security forces or neighbors.” In this context, she says, more and more people are asking for care for mental health problems. Some do not request it explicitly, but would actually need it.

Migrating is an obstacle course that takes a toll not only on bodies but also on mental health. Léa stresses that every phase of migration is traumatic: before crossing the border, during the crossing, and also on arrival. Migrants are experiencing wars, sometimes death and distress.

As a result, they are more likely to develop post-traumatic stress, depression and anxiety. On top of this, there is the case of people who already had mental health problems beforehand and can no longer be followed up or treated correctly. 

So how do authorities take that into account? Let’s be clear: access to psychosocial care is very limited in the support provided to migrants.

Legislation varies from one EU member state to another, because there is no common European legislation on mental health care for new arrivals. 

Read more

Merz, Meloni and the EU: How political attacks on rescue charities are leaving migrants to drown

What happens is that the measures in place often apply only to those with refugee status. There is often no care at all while people wait for a decision on their case. This takes months, if not years.

What’s more, the language barrier and the fear of being deported often make it harder for people to speak openly and ask for help. In Ceuta, healthcare centres, or workers, are often difficult to access because of harassment from security forces, neighbours or, sometimes, the far-right. 

For example, Léa recalls that one time when taking migrants to Médecins du Monde, they were forced to stop and get out of the car. The migrants believed for a few minutes that they were going to be deported. She describes how they were subjected to racist remarks, while the authorities refused to call Médecins du Monde to check that they were indeed heading there, preferring to arrest them.

That’s why taking care of mental health cannot go without recognising the most basic human rights.

Read more

‘Let me die’: tortured migrants and rescue ships face off against EU-sponsored Libyan forces

The problem is that politics seems to go in the opposite direction: Several NGOs and mental health organizations have already pointed out that tighter border controls, temporary reception facilities and, more broadly, the hardening of migration policies risk worsening psychosocial distress. They also make it even harder to identify vulnerable people with mental health problems.

So what do we do about it? In Sweden, Red Cross trauma centres treat refugees whatever their papers say, with interpreters in the room. In Ireland, a charity offers free counselling with no documents needed, and they insist that nothing is shared with immigration. In Germany, no less than fifty centres help survivors of torture, war and forced displacement.

Those places care for everyone in their own language, without fear, factors that are essential to supporting migrants’ mental health.

One last word to conclude: the struggle migrants face surely complicates their integration. But more importantly: this struggle doesn’t disappear when their status is cleared. 

Even when allowed to stay legally on the territory, they face racism and discrimination, further poisoning their integration and thus feeding the far right discourse.

]]> After students voted out Vučić, can Serbia’s uprising against ‘evil’ change how the state really works? https://euobserver.com/247121/after-students-voted-out-vucic-can-serbias-uprising-against-evil-change-how-the-state-really-works/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:05:11 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247121 The student movement's triumph over Aleksandar Vučić has built an unprecedented pro-democracy political momentum in Serbia. Their win follows two years of government crackdowns on protests kick-started by the Novi Sad railway station disaster two years ago.]]> It is evening a few days after the Serbian election, and young people have gathered in central Belgrade.

The group has laid out paints and brushes on the pavement. Until a few days ago, the building had been graffitied with insults towards student protesters.

A young woman writes a student protest slogan on the wall in Serbian: “Love is in the streets.” It is one of the slogans that accompanied the student protests.

“We are trying to turn the city into a kind of gallery,” explained 17-year-old student protester Adam.

He wants to wipe away insulting graffiti covering Belgrade’s streets.

“It was a truly difficult struggle. I took part in student blockades and in almost every protest. We are proud Serbia managed to defeat the system breathing down our necks for the last 14 years,” Adam said.

Serbia is processing the student movement’s triumph over then-president Aleksandar Vučić.

As students repainted the streets, police arrested the head of criminal police on suspicion of abuse of office, while the director of public broadcaster RTS resigned after being accused of spreading pro-government propaganda.

Read more

Serbia’s Student List has been inspirational, but the big test will be forming a stable anti-corruption government

Protests commemorate station tragedy

Students were beginning to gather outside the Faculty of Law at the University of Belgrade. Among them were people old enough to be those students’ grandparents. It was Friday, five days after the Student List’s election victory on Sunday (25 October).

A busy road runs past the university, with cars and public transport travelling in both directions. As 11:52 approached, those gathering outside the faculty stepped onto the road to stop traffic.

Two years prior, Novi Sad railway station had collapsed at 11:52, killing 16 people. Serbia’s residents commemorated victims with a symbolic 16 minutes of silence.

]]> Trump’s mid-term election disaster is not good news for Nato or Ukraine https://euobserver.com/247149/trumps-mid-term-election-disaster-is-not-good-news-for-nato-or-ukraine/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247149 European governments may draw the wrong lesson. Americans voted on Tuesday about inflation, the Iran war and Trump himself, not about European security. Europe should not behave as if they had.]]> Donald Trump asked Americans to “pretend” he was on the ballot. They took him at his word. 

Democrats won both chambers of Congress and flipped seven Republican Senate seats, some of them held by the party for decades. Trump had said in advance what he would do if this happened: he would veto everything.

Europeans who were cheering for the Democrats can celebrate. For Europe, though, little is likely to shift, at least for now.

Diplomats in Brussels expected little to change, and said so before the vote.

Governments may still draw the wrong lesson. The Democrats have won the power to restrain Trump, but they cannot make American policy toward Europe predictable.

Read more

Lame duck or angry duck? Europe’s leadership largely silent on Trump’s election disaster, fearing backlash

Congress can only slow Trump down

A presidential veto override needs two-thirds of both chambers, and in the Senate most ordinary bills still need 60 votes to get past a filibuster. Democrats have neither. They will control spending bills and they can subpoena officials. 

They can also block or delay nominees, which is enough to slow the administration down but not enough to run foreign policy from Capitol Hill.

Congress already authorised $400m [€356m] a year for Ukraine security assistance in 2026 and 2027, in the defence law it passed last December.

Democrats can push actual money through must-pass spending bills. A president cannot lawfully refuse to spend appropriated funds for policy reasons. 

Presidential drawdowns from US stocks, delivery schedules and export licences remain largely in executive hands.

Trump lost his emergency tariffs in the Supreme Court in February. He replaced them with a temporary global levy. When that expired on 24 July, new tariffs on imports from 60 economies took effect the same day, under a different law.

Congress could rewrite the powers it delegated to the president, but that bill would meet a veto. Even Joe Biden, a president friendly to Europe, needed months to ease the steel tariffs after Trump’s first term, and he replaced them with quotas, not free trade.

On Iran, war powers resolutions face the same veto, and attaching conditions to war money is politically hard while American troops are in the field. Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz carried oil and petroleum products equal to about a fifth of world consumption.

Most of it went to Asia, but major disruptions still push up the prices Europeans pay.

Nato withdrawal? Untested

On Nato membership itself, the protection is stronger. A 2023 provision co-written by Marco Rubio, then a Republican senator from Florida and now Trump’s secretary of state, bars withdrawal from Nato without two-thirds of the Senate or an act of Congress.

Whether it holds against a president who claims treaty withdrawal as his own power has never been tested in court.

Congress went further a year ago. The December 2025 defence law limits what Pentagon money can be used for in Europe. It cannot pay for cutting US forces there below 76,000 for more than 45 days. Nor can it pay for removing major equipment, giving up bases, or handing the top Nato command to a non-American. 

The Pentagon can still do any of this, but only after the secretary of defense and the US commander in Europe each certify the decision to Congress, submit the required assessments and then wait 60 days.

The restriction applies to fiscal 2026 funds, and Congress is considering whether to extend it.

Even if it survives, the law covers what is stationed in Europe. What Washington sends when a crisis comes, and whether aircraft based in Germany fly for European purposes or for operations somewhere else, is still decided in the White House and the Pentagon.

Hegseth holds the cards

The timing is bad too.

The Pentagon’s review of US forces in Europe was to give secretary of defense Pete Hegseth at least four sets of options by 6 November, with the review finished in December.

The new Congress only meets on 3 January, so Hegseth is scheduled to have the options weeks before any Democrat chairs a committee.

Before the vote, there was a nagging fear in Europe that a Trump beaten at home would look for distraction abroad.

Read more

Trump likely to lash out in foreign policy if Democrats take Congress, warns ex-US ambassador to EU

Josef Braml, the European director of the Trilateral Commission, warned on Wednesday (4 November) that the president may now push harder on tariffs, Nato and Ukraine.

That may very well happen. But Europe’s own response is the more immediate concern.

Europe now has rules that favour its own defence industry, in the European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP) and in the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loans. The rules alone will not produce refuelling tankers or missile stocks. That takes money and years.

A Congress more supportive of Nato and Ukraine could give governments an excuse to delay the expensive decisions that would make European defence less dependent on Washington.

Trump’s term ends in January 2029, and the Democratic majority may last only two years. Europe cannot plan its defence around a two-year American election cycle.

Americans voted on Tuesday about inflation, the Iran war and Trump himself, not about European security. Europe should not behave as if they had.

]]> [Investigation] How the EU’s methane rules came undone, and ended up giving Trump exactly what he wanted https://euobserver.com/247183/investigation-how-the-eus-methane-rules-came-undone/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247183 The Trump administration wanted the EU’s methane rules gone. Internal documents show how the commission tried, and failed, to hold the line.]]> EU ambassadors will try for a third time on Friday (6 November) to agree whether to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil and gas imports by one year or three.

Methane, a potent greenhouse gas, has become a major target of both climate regulation and industry lobbying. Capturing it is one of the “quickest and cheapest ways to curb global greenhouse gas emissions”, according to the International Energy Agency.

For many months, the EU Commission vowed it would not reopen the rules. Yet in October, Europe’s methane rules, adopted in 2024 and due to start in two months, still ended up on the chopping block. Here’s the story of how we got here.

Creole Spirit

At a summit in Pittsburgh in late February, co-hosted by US gas lobby group LNG Allies, the EU’s top energy official, Ditte Juul Jørgensen, toasted a decade of transatlantic gas trade.

In a keynote prepared by her team, she recalled how, ten years earlier, the first cargo of US liquefied natural gas (LNG) to Europe had crossed the Atlantic from Louisiana on a ship called the Creole Spirit.

It was “a most fitting name” for a ship that “embodied both the energy heritage of Louisiana and the new spirit of transatlantic partnership”, reads her speech. Later that day, she sat on a panel on the EU methane rules with US gas lobbyists.

LNG Allies later said she had “captured the spirit of the Transatlantic LNG Partnership perfectly”, calling her “a true friend of US LNG” who “graciously accepted nearly every speaking invitation we extended”.

As the commission’s top energy official since 2019, she had steered the EU through the Russian gas crisis and a more than fivefold increase in US LNG imports, which perhaps explains her warm welcome in Pittsburgh.

But to her also fell the task of defending the EU’s methane rules against a multipronged attack from the US oil and gas industry and an increasingly hostile Trump administration.

Jørgensen’s speech is one of 55 documents released by the commission’s energy department under a freedom of information request by climate research group ARIA and shared with EUobserver.

They include briefings, speeches and emails from the commission’s dealings with US officials and industry between March 2025 and May 2026. US dislike of the rules has been no secret. Trump officials and allied industry groups attacked them openly and regularly.

But the documents offer insight into how the commission tried to handle that pressure, mostly by offering industry and Washington technical fixes, even after it had become clear the Trump administration simply wanted the rules gone.

]]> Internal energy papers show “half-hearted” EU commission efforts to save methane rules https://euobserver.com/247205/leaked-energy-papers-show-half-hearted-eu-commission-efforts-to-save-methane-rules/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247205 As ambassadors meet again to decide how long to delay the EU’s methane rules, internal documents show how the commission did too little to save them.]]> For the third time in a matter of weeks, EU ambassadors will try on Friday (6 November) to agree whether to delay the EU’s methane rules for oil and gas imports by one year or by three.

Big Oil, the Trump administration and a growing group of member states have been pushing for a delay, citing supply and legal risks.

For a long time the commission refused to propose a delay, but in October it finally buckled and proposed one year.

Much of what led up to that has been reported, including on our pages. But we obtained 55 internal documents from the commission’s energy department that show how it tried to handle the pressure, and eventually failed.

They cover more than a year, from the first talks with the Trump administration in March 2025 to the spring of 2026.

US dislike of the rules has not been a secret. Trump officials and allied industry groups attacked the EU methane regulation openly and regularly. 

Climate wise there is a lot at stake. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas that traps around 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide over 20 years. A lot of it leaks into the atmosphere from wells, pipelines and gas terminals.

]]> Listen: Drug trafficking is ramping up in Europe, why and what are the consequences ?  https://euobserver.com/247225/listen-drug-trafficking-is-ramping-in-europe-why-and-what-are-the-consequences/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:09:27 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247225 The trial of 5 men suspected of brutal killings associated with France’s major drug cartel should come to an end in Aix-en Provence this Friday (6th of November).]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

The trial of 5 men suspected of brutal killings associated with France’s major drug cartel should come to an end in Aix-en Provence this Friday (6th of November).

France has been particularly affected by the ramp up of drug trafficking and related violences across Europe in recent years. But how has drug trafficking transformed into one of the major threats to European security? And what solutions are put forward in Europe?

While during the 60s-70s, European port cities like Marseille were transit zones for drugs directed to the North American market, Europe is now a key consumer market for production, which is exploding too.

Western and Central Europe is currently the second largest cocaine market in the world according to the UN’s office on drugs and crime. And levels of use are clearly increasing since 2015. 

When it comes to Eastern Europe, it has the highest prevalence of people who inject drugs worldwide : 1.3 percent in 2024.

In parallel, the quantity of drugs seized in the EU between 2014 and 2024 has surged dramatically: the amount of seized methamphetamine multiplied by 11, and five times more cocaine. 

Read more

From the Netherlands to Sierra Leone: EU aid, a president’s daughter and Europe’s most‑wanted cocaine boss

A recent investigation by the Guardian directly links the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe with the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe and the close ties they’ve forged with local mafias.

This intensification of drug trafficking in Europe, has been accompanied by a surge in correlated violences. The 2023 Eurojust report signalled that half of all homicides recorded in Europe were directly connected to drug trafficking.

Here in Brussels, 74 shootings were recorded  between January and September 2026, resulting in two deaths and 28 injuries. 

So what should we do about it ?

Last month, the European Parliament voted a resolution demanding a coordinated EU crackdown on drug trafficking networks. The resolution demands more funding on police equipment, tighter security at ports and a deepening of collaboration between customs, law enforcement and judicial authorities across the bloc.

But while nationally, right and far-right politicians call for harsher punitive approaches – other voices call for alternative solutions.

Read more

Brussels’ drug war in Saint-Gilles: residents caught between bombs, shootings and an absent state

One of these voices is anti-mafia French activist Amine Kessaci. The Marseille-born 23 year old is the brother of one of the victims of the 3 killings currently on trial. Recruited by a drug gang as a teenager, his brother Brahim was shot and burned in a car in 2020.

Now part of the French Green party, Kessaci argues that drug gangs “fill a void” left by a lack of public services, offering an illusion of economic opportunities to teenagers from economically precarious families, who feel abandoned by the school system and entrapped in the margins of society.

Similarly, Belgium’s national commissary to drugs Ine Van Wymersch underlines that the one third of young Brusselers living under the poverty line, are particularly vulnerable to criminal organisations which consider them as an “easy-to-recruit” and “disposable” workforce.

Van Wymersch warns against the counter-productive effects of repressive approaches and calls to “transform the living environment of vulnerable youth” by supporting parents, offering better access to public neighbourhood structures and creating better adapted work experience opportunities.

Van Wymersch’s recommendations also include the creation of a “Child File” from birth to detect risk factors such as poverty, family histories of crime, and low levels of education. ]]> Chinese spy suspect walks free after Prague court acquittal, while Czech spy suspect in China remains behind bars https://euobserver.com/246959/chinese-spy-suspect-walks-free-after-prague-court-acquittal-while-czech-spy-suspect-in-china-remains-behind-bars/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:01:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246959 Yang Yiming, a suspected Chinese spy, has walked free after a Czech court acquitted him, but prosecutors have appealed the verdict. However, Czech national Aleš K. is still behind bars in China for allegedly breaching the country's security laws.]]> First published in Respekt.

Yang Yiming, a suspected Chinese spy, has walked free after his arrest earlier this year in the Czech Republic.

Prague Municipal Court judge Tome Frankič found that Yiming posed as a foreign correspondent for a Chinese media outlet while working for the country’s intelligence services. He accepted assignments to covertly pass on information he obtained about politicians and other public figures.

And yet, the man was released this week on Monday (2 November). In the view of judge Frankič, the evidence against Yiming did not show he broke the law.

Read more

Czech businessman detained by Beijing faces espionage charges and could be part of swap with Chinese spy

Suspected Chinese spy walks free

In court, the prosecution failed to prove Yiming had “intentionally endangered or damaged the constitutional order, territorial integrity, defence or security of the Czech Republic, or undermined its sovereignty.”

The trial of the Chinese man was the first of its kind in modern-day Czech Republic.

Previously, espionage could be prosecuted only if police or intelligence services could prove that a person had obtained classified information such as government documents or intelligence-service materials.

But the Czech security community argued for years that defining the offence of spying was defined too narrowly, and could not adequately tackle espionage.

Indeed, collecting information on people’s private lives – whether it be their alcoholism or intimate relationships – could be enough to blackmail some to advance the interests of foreign powers.

So the previous Czech government passed a new, broader criminal offence – unauthorised activity for a foreign power.

    The same speech launched Project Meridian, a 120-day study of the technologies the US military will need for future wars. The project will be led by tech oligarch Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey (CEO of defence firm Anduril), and US politician Newt Gingrich, with the group’s findings due in January. 

    Ethical and commercial issues abound. SpaceX is a backbone of US national security, and Anduril sells jammers, interceptors, and un-crewed combat aircraft to the US military.

    Critics have noted that Musk and Luckey would be identifying needs that their own companies already meet, and the announcement describes no recusal or disclosure mechanism.

    Others, such as professor Elke Schwarz from the. Queen Mary University of London, have long shown how the commercial logic of technology firms shapes the ethics of violent technologies, treating moral and legal questions as engineering problems to be optimised away.

    From a technical and legal perspective, this is neither possible nor desirable. Project Meridian promises that this logic will set the agenda. 

    What this agenda fails to cover is just as consequential. The US administration of president Donald Trump has dismantled the machinery that teaches militaries about civilian harm.

    The Pentagon’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence fell from 40 staff to nine in 2025, and the Pentagon’s own inspector general concluded the department no longer has the personnel and capabilities needed to meet its legal responsibilities.

    Organisations like Airwars, which document civilian harm from military operations, find themselves offering evidence to commands that have almost no one left to receive it, let alone learn lessons to improve practices over time. 

    Autonomy and AI-enabled targeting depend on high quality data and feedback. A system is only as good as what its operators learn from its errors.

    Research on the quantification logics of targeting, and on outdated intelligence feeding strike decisions, shows how easily speed and scale displace the judgment that precautions require.

    Accelerating autonomy while abandoning the ability to learn from past practices does not produce a more precise or legitimate military.

    This issue is relevant to discussions in Geneva because technology that is built, bought and normalised in Washington is sold elsewhere.

    European militaries integrate, procure and operate alongside American systems.

    Precautions must be built in at the design stage, with deliberate friction where speed would erode judgment, meaningful human decision-making, and sustained engagement among developers, lawyers, and operators.

    Trump likely to lash out in foreign policy if Democrats take Congress, warns ex-US ambassador to EU

    The win is nevertheless a significant rebuttal of Trump’s MAGA coalition that has so far defined his presidency.

    Democrats took 54 seats in the Senate (out of 100) and 228 in the House (out of 435). According to the New York Times, the Democrat congressional take-over is the largest for either party since 1976.

    Trump had told voters ahead of the election to pretend he was on the ballot. Once the results were announced, he posted on Truth Social that he wasn’t on the ballot.

    Trump is still pro-Putin, anti-EU, pro-tariffs, and is struggling to find an exit ramp on the Iran war that has embroiled his administration in a possible never-ending war.

    This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. Visit account.euobserver.com/membership

    ]]>         [Interview] ‘It’s now or never’ for enlargement, Montenegro’s former EU ambassador warns https://euobserver.com/246762/interview-its-now-or-never-for-enlargement-montenegros-former-eu-ambassador-warns/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:52:40 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246762 "With the Russian intervention in Ukraine, the geopolitical situation changed dramatically ... the EU understood they have to fortify 'their territory' in south-eastern Europe, and now you have, again, full energy [in the enlargement process]," Bojan Šarkić said.]]> If internal EU politics were to block Montenegro’s accession in 2028, it would risk killing Western Balkans enlargement and leaving a “black hole” in Europe, a veteran diplomat from Podgorica told EUobserver.

    “I’m afraid it’s now or never,” said Bojan Šarkić, Montenegro’s former ambassador to the EU from 2016 to 2020.

    “If it doesn’t happen, that would be a very bad signal to everyone in the region. The reaction would be: ‘Look at these Montenegrins. They did everything they were asked to do by the EU and what did they get? Nothing’,” he added.

    “It would confirm what eurosceptics in the region have been saying – and there are quite a few of them. Just switch on Serbian TV, every day you hear: ‘The EU is falling apart. Look at the demonstrations in France’,” he said.

    “And all this creates fertile soil for interference by other countries,” Šarkić said, referring to Russia.

    The 67-year-old diplomat, who retired last year, spoke to EUobserver as the European Commission prepared to publish its annual reports on the 10 candidate countries in line to join the 27-nation bloc one day – the six Western Balkan states, Georgia, Moldova, Turkey, and Ukraine.

    Šarkić began his diplomatic career in the former Yugoslavia in 1987, spent four years in Moscow in what was then the Soviet Union, before being sent to London and Brussels.

    Croatia was the last country to join the EU, in 2013.

    Following the EU’s migration crisis in 2015, enlargement appetite waned, while Turkey’s post-coup crackdown in 2016 saw its talks put on hold.

    In the past two years, democratic backsliding in Georgia and Serbia also saw their talks frozen.

    But at the same time, Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022 created a new geopolitical imperative to save the Western Balkans and post-Soviet states from becoming what Šarkić called a “black hole” of instability and Russian meddling in Europe.

    The EU fast-tracked Moldova and Ukraine’s accession bids, while Armenia also peeled away from Russia and now aimed to formally apply for membership, in 2027 or 2028.

    “In my time in Brussels, I had top politicians in the EU, in the Council, in the European Commission, telling me to forget about becoming a member of the EU in the forthcoming future,” said Šarkić.

    “And while the EU was slow and lazy on enlargement, Russia was not lazy at all in trying to build its influence in the region,” he said.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/nasdaq-heading-for-worst-day-in-18-months-as-wall-street-sustains-widespread-losses</link>
      <description><p>Nearly $2tn shaved off Nasdaq value as worries of curbs to AI datacenters ripple across bourses</p><p>The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs that the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/05/democrats-state-legislatures-midterm-elections">midterm election</a> results.</p><p>As Wall Street sustained widespread losses, the Nasdaq composite tumbled into “correction territory” – more than 10% below its recent record high – with more than $2tn shaved off its value by the end of trading Thursday. The tech-heavy index had<strong> </strong>its biggest one-day fall since Donald Trump announced his “liberation day” tariffs on US trading partners in April 2025.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/nasdaq-heading-for-worst-day-in-18-months-as-wall-street-sustains-widespread-losses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Rural voters were feeling left behind before the midterms, poll shows</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy</link>
      <description><p>Polling done for the Guardian shows plummeting support from a former key constituency of Donald Trump’s base</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/nov/05/what-happens-after-the-blue-wave-our-reporters-answer-your-midterm-election-results-questions">Q&amp;A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>Polling conducted by the Harris Poll for the Guardian before the election shows just how angry voters were and points to one key reason Republicans lost so badly: plummeting support from rural voters, once a key constituency of Donald Trump’s base.</p><p>Over the summer, 95% of Americans indicated they believed there was an <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/jul/07/cost-of-living-poll-groceries-gas">affordability crisis</a>, particularly because of steep gas and grocery prices. By October, 61% of voters <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">believed</a> the country was experiencing a recession, even though technically it wasn’t.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/former-trump-voters-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears</link>
      <description><p>Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/04/midterm-elections-results-senate-house-michigan-maine-mississippi-latest-updates">US midterm elections – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/explainer-midterms-trump-us-global-economy-markets">After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?</a></p></li></ul><p>US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a>, lifted by hopes that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.</p><p>The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&amp;P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">won control</a> of the Senate and the House of Representatives.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/05/tech-barons-america-musk-bezos-zuckerberg</link>
      <description><p>Democrats’ success was helped by popular anger over tech, AI and the super rich – life for billionaires could become much more difficult</p><p>The photo of Silicon Valley centibillionaires at Donald Trump’s inauguration – Musk, Bezos and Zuckerberg, front row and side by side – now looks like a hitlist for a blue Congress hellbent on making life difficult for billionaires.</p><p>The picture symbolized at the time the bending of the knee by the richest men in the world to its most powerful, a symbiosis of the ultra-rich. Already unfathomably wealthy, Silicon Valley tycoons believed a Maga-sized public shift to the right would enrich them even more. It did. For several years, while Trump seemed an everlasting kingmaker and AI’s expansion seemed unstoppable, their fortunes ballooned to values beyond comprehension. Elon Musk’s surpassed $1tn.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/05/tech-barons-america-musk-bezos-zuckerberg">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires</link>
      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel prize-winning economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton once <a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1011492107">proposed that</a> rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money.</p><p>They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe betide the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires">Continue reading...</a></description>
