Wireless chargers are being deployed in a number of indoor and outdoor applications for charging the mobile robots. | Credit: WiBotic

As robot fleets scale, charging becomes an operational challenge. Understanding how to optimize charging for fleets of mobile robots is key to getting the best performance from the fleet throughout the day.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic

With growing deployments, charging is becoming more than a question of how long a battery lasts or how quickly it can recharge. Charging strategy can affect fleet uptime, facility infrastructure, maintenance requirements, and even the size of the batteries that robot manufacturers need to carry.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic, recently joined The Robot Report Podcast to discuss how those considerations are changing as robot fleets scale.

He also discussed opportunity charging, the tradeoffs around fast charging, WiBotic’s move toward higher-power systems, and how charging data could help operators identify power problems.

This is an excerpt from the podcast interview. Listen to the full audio anywhere you get your podcasts or online in the show notes.

WiBotic expands beyond its traditional robotics markets

What has changed recently at WiBotic, and how is the market maturing?

Waters: Overall, WiBotic has diversified into a few different markets, but all the while, robotics has really been growing, as we all know, over the last last one to two years for sure.

That was a big motivator for us to pursue getting into some adjacent markets. Take, for example, floor care, medical carts, space, and defense applications, all of which are markets that really use the same product as our longstanding robotics customers from a wireless charging, autonomous charging perspective.

Flash-forward a year of focusing on that and putting all the internal operational, sales, and engineering teams in place to support different markets. Here we are a year and a half later, and robotics is booming everywhere you look, right? I mean, all of our legacy customers in robotics have had significant volume growth this year.

We are seeing huge growth in automotive AMR adoption. We are seeing growth in outdoor robotic inspection for energy substations, and a lot of outdoor applications are growing. And then there’s the wild card of humanoids.

Wireless charging is a really interesting dynamic in humanoids as far as what it can enable and how it can improve uptime and eliminate some of these Achilles’ heels issues that humanoids have around downtime.

Opportunity charging changes the equation for large robot fleets

As fleets of mobile robots grow, where does charging start creating operational friction?

Waters: The big trend as charging relates to operational impact is what we’ve probably talked about before with Gene [Demaitre]. WiBotic has always looked at as a great opportunity for wireless charging. But, you know, it takes a while for fleets to get big enough for it to truly make sense. And I think we’re finally at that place. And what I’m referring to is opportunity charging.

So it’s the concept of “Don’t just put the chargers on the sides of the factories.” And then when the battery on the robot gets to 20%, that robot might be on the far side of the factory. Now it’s got to drive 10 minutes while watching out for everything else and while being ignored by the fleet management for doing a task, even though it’s in an area where a task needs to get done, right? Because it has to go charge.

That strategy, which is arguably easier to implement at a small scale, because you can truly just say, “If any one of these robots’ batteries hits 20%, stop and go drive to the charging station.” That’s fairly easy to implement. That gets really complicated, and that leads to a lot of unwanted downtime when the fleets start to get bigger. Even like fleets of 20 to 40, this becomes a bottleneck.

We need to implement opportunity charging. And it doesn’t make sense to do opportunity charging with anything but wireless. Because if you did it with contacts, your robots would be hitting the contacts so many more times. And even if you had the world’s most strongest contact, it still would require maintenance at some point, times all of the chargers in your fleet.

If the robot does a task and it’s got 10 seconds to sit there, well, a charging station should be positioned right where that robot naturally is going to sit.

You could look at that as well. It’s only charging for 10 seconds, but if you do that often enough, it’s adding substantial energy back into the batteries across the fleet and allowing these things to run 24/7.

You can completely eliminate that. Just allow the robots to stay in the loops where they’re operating when you employ opportunity charging. So that’s really the trend that we’ve been seeing and the demand we’ve been getting, and the main reason why companies are looking for wireless power.

How should companies think about charging during system design instead of treating it as an accessory at the end?

Waters: If I boil it down to three things, I think companies should be thinking about power infrastructure. I’ll come back to a few details on these. Where are your electrical outlets, and how many of them do you have, and are they rated for enough power to handle all the chargers you want to deploy? So think about that up front. That bites people. We’ve seen a lot when you think about that too late.

I think people are really questioning. How big of a battery do I need? Do I need a battery that supports an eight-hour runtime? Do I need a battery that supports super fast charging? In the world of batteries, most of these types of things trade off with each other.

They might be overdesigning it. They might be adding way too much battery cost for what they really need, especially if they’re thinking about charging strategies.

We still hear a lot of customers be like, “We need to charge these things as fast as humanly possible.” And we’re going to listen, and we’re going to assume the customers made the right choices for the right reasons.

It’s not our job necessarily to push back, but we are curious battery guys, and we’re a friendly company to work with. So we sometimes ask: “Do you really want to charge at 3°C all the time? Have you seen a data sheet from the battery manufacturer that says what that’s gonna do to lifetime? Is that worth it?”

And then the third thing for sure is maintenance. If you wait till you’ve already finished your design, and you’re starting to deploy and haven’t thought about those things, then almost surely, you will get bit by every one of those things within at least a couple of months, if not sooner.

Right now, we are actively developing more around two areas of innovation. One is size and weight. We are seeing a lot of interest in drone applications. WiBotic certainly has had a long history with drones.

We’re developing lightweight, high-power systems for drones, which just so happens to be kind of the same thing that humanoids need as well.

As fleets of mobile robots grow, the need for interoperability among systems increases. The Association for Advancing Automation, or A3, yesterday published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communications among industrial mobile robots, or IMRs, regardless of vendor or model.

“Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor,” stated Carole Franklin, director of standards development for robotics at A3. “Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years.”

“Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located,” she added. “This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.”

ISO 21423 addresses IMR interoperability

Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability provides a common set of requirements for automated guided vehicles (AGVs), autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and similar systems from different suppliers operating in the same facility.

The new standard specifies how IMRs, fleet managers, and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with one another, A3 explained.

For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning, which improves robot availability and system efficiency, asserted A3. A common protocol could increase competition in the market and support innovation, it said. One benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world.

Standard also covers communications with other systems

ISO 21423 also covers communication with machines tended by robots; enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools; and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors, and alarms. People using or wearing mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots.

“ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in robotics standardization efforts,” said the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization. The standard is available at the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320.

ThermAffyx both securely positions and warms patients during robot-assisted surgeries. Source: Gentherm

Many healthcare advances come from within that industry, but innovations from other industries can also find a role. Gentherm Medical has designed its ThermAffyx Patient Safety System based on thermal management experience from the automotive industry.

The system both securely positions a patient and provides patient warming for robot-assisted surgery. Gentherm Inc. said ThermAffyx does both while minimizing the amount of space required and without the need for forced-air equipment.

The Novi, Mich.-based company launched the system at the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses (AORN) Global Surgical Conference this year. Gentherm noted that numerous medical professionals told it that “almost all of their robotics patients are hypothermic.”

Adam Hauke, global director for product strategy and innovation at Gentherm, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report.

Gentherm addresses Trendelenburg challenge

What is the challenge that ThermAffyx addresses, and how are patient positioning and hypothermia handled conventionally?

Hauke: The ThermAffyx Patient Safety System combines active patient warming and secure positioning into a single solution, helping address two critical perioperative challenges: maintaining normothermia and reducing patient movement during surgery.

The current standard of care consists of forced-air warming solutions and a securement pad. Historically, warming and positioning have been addressed independently because, in many surgical procedures, they do not significantly interfere with one another. However, that’s not the case in most robotic-assisted surgeries.

These procedures frequently require patients to remain in Trendelenburg positioning, where the body is tilted head-down to provide surgical access to the pelvis and lower abdomen. Patients may remain in these positions for extended periods while robotic systems are docked and utilized.

This positioning introduces several challenges, including increased pressure and shear forces that can contribute to pressure injuries, the potential for nerve-related complications if positioning is not optimized, and the risk of patient movement or shifting during lengthy procedures. Underbody securement pads are designed to address these positioning challenges.

At the same time, maintaining normothermia becomes more challenging because robotic equipment occupies the physical space that traditional over-body warming solutions must be deployed in. In these situations, clinicians often rely on under-body warming approaches, but they are difficult or impossible to use in robotics because they would interfere with the underbody securement pads used for safely positioning the patient.

Suddenly, warming and positioning are no longer separate considerations. They are competing for the same real estate.

How much do patients move around during surgical procedures?

Hauke: In the routine course of things in the operating room, “patient movement” is not tracked. “Patient movement,” if it is recorded it is done so as “light anesthesia.” It is usually referring to if the patient’s anesthetic wears off prematurely and they move a hand or leg type thing.

No one is measuring anything on the OR table related to patient movement, as everything is under the sterile drape at that point. The only way the surgical team knows if a patient moves, is if there is tension on the robotic instruments typically.

Any unintended patient movement during robot-assisted surgeries can vary greatly based on a number of factors. There are multiple contributing individual factors such as patient weight, height, and body proportions, as well as procedure-based factors such as the patient position, the steepness the OR table is tilted to and whether or not other positioning solutions are used such as stirrups.

If there is a shift related to Trendelenburg, it’s usually noticed by anesthesia as difficult respirations or a drop in capnography. An actual measurable shift in a patient on the OR table doesn’t occur very often and is not currently a recorded stat.

Submit your innovation now!

Is there a weight or size range for the system?

Hauke: The ThermAffyx System is intended for adult patients and has been tested on individuals up to 297 lb. [134.7 kg]. The Pad is designed so that a patient can be positioned anywhere within the heating zone to receive active warming.

The Pad’s safety sensors do not require direct patient contact to function. As always, clinicians should follow their facility’s protocols and guidelines for safe patient positioning.

Does Gentherm’s system require more power than existing setups?

Hauke: No, ThermAffyx runs on standard hospital electrical outlets.

Is there any danger of thermal or electromagnetic interference with certain surgical instruments?

Hauke: We have mitigated the risks of compatibility with other devices as far as possible. The system has been designed and verified to comply with all applicable industry standards and FDA guidance — including compatibility with electrocautery, diathermy, defibrillation equipment, RFID devices, wireless power transfer devices, and 5G cellular networks. Therefore, the risk of thermal or EM interference is low.

However, there is always residual risk of issues occurring. We do not control the design and use of external devices that may be used in combination with ThermAffyx, and thus cannot guarantee other devices have been designed to meet the same standards or that devices are being used per the manufacturer’s labeling.

ThermAffyx moves toward the market

How is the system progressing toward commercialization?

Hauke: Commercialization is well under way. Our teams are in active trials across the country with strong adoption in both new accounts and our legacy Gentherm accounts.

How difficult was it to get U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearance?

Hauke: Although Gentherm is an expert in patient warming devices, gaining FDA clearance for ThermAffyx took careful development planning and execution. This is the first and only all-in-one product to have Class II indications for use for maintaining normothermia and securement.

To ensure the proper steps were being taken, we started the process with a Q-Sub to the FDA to receive their feedback on our claims and validation plan. We then implemented the appropriate design and testing per the FDA feedback to validate our claims.

An additional requirement with the FDA is to prove the usability of your device. The operation of the device must fit flawlessly into clinicians’ regular workflows to ensure the system can be used safely without introducing complexity. Nurses and anesthesiologists provided critical inputs to the design through focus groups, then validated the design in extensive hands-on usability studies.

Does this add to the cost of OR equipment or surgical procedures?

Hauke: While ThermAffyx does add incremental cost for the technology — lower than most capital budget thresholds — the more important consideration is its potential impact on reducing costly downstream complications.

By helping to reduce the risk of unintended perioperative hypothermia, patient movement or pressure related injuries, the system may help avoid adverse events that can increase length of stay, require additional treatment, and drive higher overall costs of care.

In robotic surgery, these procedures are already supported by established reimbursement structures and procedure codes, making this technology a natural fit within the existing surgical workflow.

Will you be selling it directly or through third parties?

Hauke: ThermAffyx is available for purchase through Gentherm’s U.S. contract sales team.

Are there other potential use cases for ThermAffyx and its component technologies?

Hauke: ThermAffyx was specifically designed to address the challenge of maintaining normothermia in patients undergoing minimally invasive and robotic-assisted procedures, particularly in gynecological, urological, or general surgery cases that require patient positioning in tilt.

However, its innovative 3-in-1 design offers benefits that extend well beyond these initial applications.

By integrating warming technology into a pressure redistributing underbody foam pad, ThermAffyx can help support patient temperature management in a wide range of surgical settings where maintaining normothermia can be difficult including orthopedics, cardiovascular, colorectal, and plastics cases.

The post 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

What AI changes about vulnerability discovery

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

  • Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot
    A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.
  • Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence
    Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.
  • Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control
    An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working.

A published patch still needs to be proven safe

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

Three questions can help teams respond:

  • Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.
  • What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.
  • How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

From discovery to safer deployment

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, watch for VicOne’s upcoming white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

]]> The European Commission has adopted the 2027 European Innovation Council (EIC) Work Programme, allocating €1.8 billion to support DeepTech startups, scale-ups and researchers across Europe.

The funding package aims to help promising technologies move from early-stage research to commercialisation, while improving access to investment for women-led and DefenceTech companies.

Ekaterina Zaharieva, Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, says: “This is how it puts our Startup and Scaleup Strategy into action: mobilising more capital, stimulating customer deals, cutting complexity, and making bold investments on the technologies that will shape our future. And, as we shape the next EU research and innovation programme, our task is to turn Europe’s scientific excellence, talent and industrial strength into new companies and lasting competitiveness.”

The programme marks the final EIC funding package under Horizon Europe 2021–2027, the EU’s research and innovation framework.

A significant part of the programme focuses on expanding access to growth capital. This includes completing the €1 billion commitment to the Scaleup Europe Fund, launched in 2026 and managed by investment firm EQT. The fund aims to attract at least €4 billion from other investors and support European technology companies through investments averaging more than €100 million.

Alongside this initiative, the EIC will continue supporting startups through its STEP Scale Up scheme, targeting companies developing strategic technologies. The 2027 programme also completes funding allocations of €200 million for defence investments and €25 million for the Advanced Innovation Challenges pilot, both introduced in 2026.

These measures form part of the EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy and the Competitiveness Compass, two initiatives intended to strengthen Europe’s innovation ecosystem and address obstacles faced by technology companies seeking to grow.

Established under Horizon Europe in 2021, the EIC has a budget exceeding €10 billion for the 2021–2027 period. Since its launch, it has supported more than 800 companies and nearly 700 research projects, providing financial assistance at different stages of technological development.

Its investment arm, the EIC Fund, has already invested close to €2 billion in more than 375 deep tech startups, attracting approximately 3.5 times that amount in co-investment.

The programme also expands support for women-led startups through a redesigned Women TechEU initiative, doubling individual grants to €150k. A new European Prize for Women Innovators in Quantum will also be introduced, complementing the existing European Prize for Women Innovators and recognising female entrepreneurs working in quantum technologies.

Another priority is helping EIC-backed startups secure their first customers. New measures will connect companies with public and private procurers, allowing them to test emerging technologies and explore potential commercial applications.

Support for dual-use and defence technologies will remain part of the EIC’s activities, reflecting the EU’s interest in strengthening its technological capabilities across strategic sectors.

At the same time, the Commission intends to reduce administrative complexity and make funding more accessible to innovators at different stages of development.

]]> Munich-based aviation startup VÆRIDION has raised €30 million in a Series A2 funding round and selected for a €94.5 million grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund, bringing the combined value to €124.5 million.

The investment round was co-led by Dutch investors SHIFT Invest and Invest-NL, with participation from existing backers World Fund, Project A and Vsquared Ventures. PAYBACK founder and DeepTech investor Alexander Rittweger also joined the round. VÆRIDION has raised approximately €60 million to date, excluding the newly announced EU grant.

Ivor van Dartel, founder and CEO of VÆRIDION, says: “Over the past year, we have turned the Microliner from a validated design into hardware, with exceptional capital efficiency. Our propulsion and battery technology is now being tested at our own facility in Oberpfaffenhofen. This equity round enables us to build our first conforming aircraft. The Commission’s selection of CAROLUS supports the next step: establishing the industrial capability for Microliner production.

“Building out of Europe, our mission is to make regional flying commercially viable and accessible again, in Europe and for operators worldwide.”

VÆRIDION’s announcement comes amid other European funding rounds for next-generation aircraft and aerospace technologies in 2026.

In France, AURA AERO announced a €50 million Series B to advance its electric and hybrid-electric aircraft programmes, while HyLight raised €13 million for hydrogen-powered autonomous airships. In the UK, Greenjets secured €35 million for aerospace propulsion technology and Skyfly raised €8.91 million for electric aircraft development.

Elsewhere, Denmark’s Acodyne secured €2.5 million for unmanned cargo aircraft, while Germany’s SPREAD AI raised €25 million for industrial engineering software serving sectors including aerospace.

Together with VÆRIDION’s €30 million equity round, these selected announcements represent approximately €164.4 million in financing, excluding VÆRIDION’s separately selected EU grant.

EU-Startups previously covered VÆRIDION’s €14 million Series A in December 2024, led by returning investor World Fund.

Daria Saharova, Managing Partner at World Fund, adds: “For the past half century, Airbus has shown that Europe can build aircraft the world buys. VÆRIDION is writing the next chapter with a fully electric aircraft, built in Bavaria, with a clear path to certification. Investing in the future of aviation is Europe’s power play, and I am proud to back Ivor and the team.”

Founded in 2021 by former Airbus manager Ivor van Dartel and headquartered in Munich, VÆRIDION is developing fully electric aircraft designed to make short-distance regional aviation more economically viable.

Its flagship aircraft, the Microliner, aims to carry nine passengers over distances of approximately 400 kilometres, connecting regional destinations that have become increasingly difficult to serve profitably using conventional aircraft.

The €30 million investment will finance the development of VÆRIDION’s first certification-conforming aircraft and further propulsion testing. Meanwhile, the €94.5 million Innovation Fund grant is intended to support the CAROLUS project, which will establish and scale up a final assembly facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, near Munich.

The project was selected from 358 applications as one of 12 large-scale projects, making VÆRIDION the only German company and the only aviation project selected in this category. The grant remains subject to the completion of an agreement expected in 2027.

The Microliner combines a glider-inspired wing with patented modular battery technology and a multi-engine propulsion system driving a single propeller. It is being developed in passenger and cargo configurations, with a targeted range of 400 kilometres carrying nine passengers under Instrument Flight Rules, or up to 550 kilometres carrying four passengers under Visual Flight Rules.

The company is targeting operating costs below €0.40 per seat-kilometre, which it believes could allow operators to offer tickets at prices comparable to first-class journeys on Germany’s ICE high-speed trains. Its broader ambition is to restore regional connections, including services linking smaller German cities and airfields that are no longer served by commercial airlines.

Thijs Gitmans, General Partner at SHIFT Invest, adds: “Regional aviation is one of the clearest cases where electrification makes both environmental and commercial sense. VÆRIDION has chosen a certification pathway regulators already understand and has delivered real hardware on a disciplined budget. We are proud to lead this round and to back a European champion in electric flight with European funding.”

The company reports customer commitments for more than 130 aircraft, representing a potential value exceeding €730 million. Its launch customer is Belgium-based ASL Group, with the first Microliner delivery targeted for 2030.

In March 2026, VÆRIDION opened its production and testing facility at Oberpfaffenhofen Airport, where it has since powered on its electric engine for the first time. The facility was acquired following the insolvency of German electric aviation startup Lilium.

The startup is now preparing to integrate its battery packs and propulsion system into a ground-testing platform known as a copper bird. Alongside wind-tunnel testing, this work will support the development of its first certification-conforming prototype, currently targeted for late 2027 or early 2028.

With engineering activities in Munich and Delft, and production planned in Bavaria, VÆRIDION intends to expand its European team as it progresses towards flight testing, certification and industrial production.

]]> Green Voltis, a Stockholm-based route-to-market (RTM) optimiser that uses AI to operate and trade battery storage across European power markets, has raised €13.5 million in a Series A round, with Lochpine Capital as the sole investor.

The company optimises standalone battery storage and co-located renewable-plus-storage projects, with more than 1.2 GWh under contract and in operation.

Martin Kievit, CEO and co-founder of Green Voltis, said, “Every new gigawatt of renewables makes Europe’s grid harder to balance, and flexibility now sets the pace of the energy transition. We built Aether and Chronos to turn storage and renewable plants into assets the grid can rely on and investors can bank on. The next wave of demand comes from AI. Data centres need power faster than grids can deliver it, and the intelligence that operates a battery can also manage a data centre’s energy. Green Voltis will provide the AI energy infrastructure layer between the grid and compute. With Lochpine Capital as a long-term partner, we are ready to build it.”

Founded in 2024 by Kievit, Ali Shi, and Gino Zhang, Green Voltis is an AI-native platform that trades, protects, and optimises renewable energy assets across markets and years. It claims to replace manual energy trading and fragmented EMS tools with a fully autonomous AI optimisation system.

According to the company, as Europe builds battery storage faster than ever, grid connections are slowing and becoming more complex, and new grid-forming requirements have added another hurdle that many control systems weren’t built for. This has led to prices across day-ahead, intraday, and balancing markets now moving every 15 minutes, making revenues hard to predict and projects harder to finance.

Green Voltis claims to cover the full path from grid connection to trading. Its engineering team handles hot commissioning and ancillary-services prequalification, so projects start earning sooner. 

Its energy management system, designed in Sweden and called Chrono, controls the site, is certified against grid codes and supports grid-forming operation. Aether AI, its trading agent built on time-series foundation models, forecasts prices and stacks revenue and capacity across several markets at the same time, rather than committing a battery to one market at a time. 

Additionally, the Swedish startup offers bankable commercial structures, including revenue sharing, tolling and revenue floors, that help owners secure project finance.

Green Voltis reported that its managed assets have consistently outperformed the Clean Horizon index, an independent benchmark for battery storage revenues. The company has market access in place or underway in 10 European countries.

The company is now applying the same capabilities to AI infrastructure. In Europe’s main data centre hubs, grid connections can take seven to ten years, and regulators from Ireland to Finland are starting to require new data centres to provide grid flexibility. 

Through its Power-to-Compute business, Green Voltis aims to connect the grid on one side and compute on the other, running data centre sites as grid-friendly flexible assets so that compute can get power sooner. It has a pipeline of around 120 MW of powered land in the Nordics and will partner with compute operators to develop it.

Blake Niu, Partner and Head of Private Equity at Lochpine Capital, said, “As renewables take a larger share of the energy mix, grid connection and power trading are becoming key to the value of energy assets, and they are among the scarcest capabilities in Europe’s energy transition.

]]> Founded in 2021, AppliedAI builds Opus, the AI transformation platform that rewires how enterprises run and ties every change to the bottom line. 

Many companies have tested AI, but few have scaled it across their workflows and systems. Opus closes this gap. Opus starts with how a process really runs today, and then redesigns it for AI. The result is a workflow built for the real world, which allows AI to scale in daily operations. Every run of the workflow and every decision, whether made by an AI agent or a person, is recorded.

Over time, this creates a digital twin of the organisation’s processes. Companies can always show what happened, why it happened, when, and based on which data. Before a project starts, Opus calculates what the new process will deliver, and it measures the result after go-live. Opus is now launching in the DACH region. The focus is on insurance, healthcare and other regulated industries, where strict rules make reliable and traceable AI especially valuable.

Why is 2026 the right moment for European enterprises to move AI from pilots to production, and why is DACH both a demanding and promising market?

AI models are no longer the bottleneck. When pilots fail, the reasons are usually operational: old systems are hard to connect, results are not measured, and there is no governance. These are exactly the problems we built Opus to solve. Opus takes an existing process, redesigns it for AI, and runs it in production with full governance and a complete audit trail. Today, this works reliably in regulated environments. That is why we are bringing Opus to DACH now.

DACH is a demanding market. Regulation is strict, data must stay in the region, and buyers expect governance from day one. But this is also what makes the market so promising. Banks, insurers and healthcare providers here run large, document-heavy back offices. This is exactly where reliable, well-governed AI creates the most value. 

What most often prevents European companies from scaling AI beyond pilots, and how should they choose the processes and solutions most likely to deliver value?

I see three main reasons why pilots stall. First, they are built on assumptions, not on the real process, so the first exception breaks them. Second, integration and governance come too late. Third, nobody owns a clear target, and often there is no way to measure success at all.

Good starting points share a few traits. The work is high-volume and repetitive. It spans several systems and involves many documents and exceptions. And someone owns the result. But the most important criterion is the return on investment. Not every process that can use AI should use AI.

AI pays off when we redesign the process, not just automate it. That is why, at Opus, we start by mapping how a process really runs today and measuring its baseline: time, cost, quality and error rates. Opus draws on its Work Knowledge Graph, a proprietary model of over a million enterprise processes organised by industry and jurisdiction. Then we calculate the expected return of the redesigned process, ideally before anything is built or changed. Once the new workflow is live, we measure again. This way, the value is clear before the project starts and provable after it goes live.

Then start with one process, prove it on real data within weeks, and expand from there. Choosing well also means knowing where AI does not belong. If an existing system already handles a process end to end, leave it alone.

Beyond cost savings, how should companies measure the success of AI-driven automation?

Cost savings are easy to report, but they are rarely the biggest benefit. I recommend five measures:

  • Capacity: Can the team handle more work without adding people?
  • Quality: How accurate is each field, for each case type? Measure this on test data that was never used for training. A single “97% accurate” number hides too much.
  • Exceptions: A high automation rate is not enough. A wrong result that slips through unnoticed is worse than one that is flagged.
  • Cycle time: How long does a case take from start to finish? Most delays come from waiting for human review, not from the machine.
  • Auditability: In regulated industries, full traceability is a result in itself.

One example from our work: with Opus, a financial regulator cut licensing reviews from weeks to minutes of structured preparation, and every step remained fully traceable.

With the EU AI Act and strict data-protection rules, how can regulated sectors such as insurance and healthcare turn compliance and governance into a competitive advantage?

Many companies see governance as a cost. I see it as the thing that lets you go live. In regulated industries, the key question is not “Can AI do this?” It is “Will this pass risk, legal and security review?”

Governance becomes an advantage when it is built in from the start. That means AI acts within clear limits, humans approve the critical steps, every action is logged, and sensitive data stays in the company’s environment. This is how we built Opus: governance is part of the foundation. Every run and every decision is recorded, and over time this builds a Digital Twin of the organisation: a living model of how the business runs and what each part of it is worth. Companies that add compliance later often cannot use AI in these processes at all.

One more point: credibility with risk teams comes from precision. Be clear about which rules apply to you, from the EU AI Act to BaFin or FINMA. And never claim more than you can prove.

As AI agents take on more complex workflows, how will the relationship between employees and AI evolve, and what role do leadership, trust, and culture play?

Nobody can say how work will look in ten years. But for the next few years, we have a clear view. AI will free up a large share of the time knowledge workers spend today on routine tasks like typing, searching and checking. We should not pretend otherwise.

The real question is what happens with that time. If companies redesign their processes now, they can create meaningful new responsibilities for these people. Employees can then focus on the work where their judgement counts and where they create real value: complex cases, difficult decisions and contact with customers.

But these new roles do not appear on their own. They must be made visible. When we map a process with Opus, we define exactly where AI does the work and where a human needs to decide. This makes the human role clear from the start, instead of leaving it to chance.

This is where leadership matters most. Leaders need to explain openly what will change, and show employees where their future role lies. Trust grows when people can see that AI works within clear limits, and when they help shape the new processes themselves. Culture follows when people experience that AI takes over routine work, not their responsibility.

Over the next three to five years, where can European businesses differentiate from the US and China in enterprise AI, and what should leaders do today to prepare?

Europe will probably not build the biggest AI models. But that is not where most value will come from. Europe’s strength is trusted, well-governed AI in regulated industries, built under its own rules and in its own languages. That is a real advantage, if leaders use it.

There are four things leaders should do now:

  1. Start with reality. Map how your processes really run today, including all the exceptions and workarounds. The process in the handbook is rarely the process people actually follow. With Opus Discover, AI agents interview the people doing the work and map how the process really runs, including the exceptions and workarounds.
  2. Define your KPIs before you start. Decide what should improve, for example cycle time, quality or capacity, and measure where you stand today. Without a baseline, you cannot prove success.
  3. Think in processes, not in tools. Don’t buy a new AI tool for every task. Look for a platform that can run many processes in one place, with one standard for governance.
  4. Plan the new roles early. Decide where people will add value once AI takes over routine work, and communicate it openly.

The winners will not be the companies with the biggest models. They will be the ones that turned AI into part of how they operate, while others were still running pilots.

]]> Kabilio, a Barcelona-based startup building an AI platform for accounting firms and the small businesses they serve, has closed a €10 million funding round. 

The round was led by Picus Capital and Visionaries; they also led Kabilio’s pre-Seed round. CDTI, Spain’s public agency for technological innovation, also participated. 

“Nobody becomes an accountant to chase receipts, and nobody starts a business to do paperwork, yet that is where so much time gets lost. We built Kabilio to let AI handle the repetitive work and the accountant stays in control. This funding takes us from automating isolated tasks, to giving firms an agent that carries out complete workflows under their direction,” said Jose Ojeda, co-founder and Co-CEO of Kabilio.

Founded in 2025 by Jose Ojeda and Álex Valls, Kabilio has developed a platform that uses generative AI to help accounting advisors and their clients modernise the way they collaborate. 

Kabilio began with pre-accounting, collecting and preparing documents and data for bookkeeping, a task typically done manually. The company says that on Kabilio, AI reads invoices and suggests how to book them, matches bank transactions, prepares the reconciliation, and flags what needs a professional’s eye, without changing the tools the firm already uses; the accountant reviews and approves rather than types.

It claims to cut time spent on bookkeeping and reconciliation by around 60%. “The rails were also built for what comes next: every document, transaction and entry is structured data, with the firm’s rules and decisions recorded alongside it, so an agent can take over the work,” the company mentioned in the press release. 

The company also announced that it is now launching its own AI accounting agent, starting with firms’ core internal workflows. The agent can retrieve invoices and statements from client emails, match and reconcile bank transactions, validate entries, and follow up on missing paperwork.

The Spanish startup also notes that in order to streamline data collection, the agent can also communicate directly with clients via email and WhatsApp to request additional documents and information. Accountants give instructions in plain language and decide, client by client, exactly how much autonomy the agent receives. 

The company also launched Kabilio Empresas in September for SMEs, which lets clients invoice, connect their bank accounts, and track cash flow on the same platform their accounting firm uses.

It also notes that information reaches the firm as soon as it’s recorded, so it works with live data year-round, not just at tax deadlines. Kabilio works only through the accounting firm, which decides which clients join the platform and what the agent does for them. Fiscalidad Inteligente and Alemany Assessors already use the technology to manage a large part of their client portfolios, Kabilio revealed. 

In a later phase, the company will extend the agent to its clients. Using the shared platform, it will issue invoices, chase late payments, and request missing receipts on behalf of business owners. It will also answer everyday tax and accounting questions in seconds, not days. 

“An agent is only as good as the data it works on. That is why we are bringing the firm’s clients onto the same platform: the moment a business issues an invoice or a payment hits its bank, the firm has it and the agent will be able to act on it. The firm is freed from busy work, and its clients feel the difference,” said Valls, co-founder and Co-CEO of Kabilio.

The company plans to use this round to fund the next phase of a plan Kabilio has followed since launch: first a system to boost accountants; next introducing an AI workforce to handle repetitive tasks under accountants’ direction; and finally, extending that workforce to the firm’s clients through a shared platform.

Kabilio will close 2026 working with more than 500 accounting firms, with notable customers including Adlanter, as well as Solfico and Gemap, part of the iusTime group. The company has grown to 80 people, more than half in product and engineering.

]]> Sequoia Capital, one of Silicon Valley’s oldest and most prominent venture capital firms, has closed its London office as part of a broader restructuring.

In an announcement titled “The Sequoia of Tomorrow”, the firm outlined several sweeping changes and confirmed that it has raised €8.89 billion ($10 billion) in new funds. The biggest announcement is that it no longer sees the need for a physical European presence. While the firm is exiting Europe, three of its four London-based partners have decided to remain in Europe rather than relocate to California.

“We are closing our London office, which means several people will be leaving Sequoia.  This is not about the team – they are excellent. We simply don’t see the need for a local presence. We believe that Europe will continue to produce outlier founders and companies, and that we can continue to provide world class support from our home base in the Bay Area,” the firm said.

Despite being offered the opportunity to move to San Francisco, three of Sequoia’s four London-based partners – Luciana Lixandru, Julien Bek, and George Robson – have opted to remain in Europe. Anas Biad is the only London-based partner who has confirmed he will relocate to the United States and remain with Sequoia.

Lixandru joined Sequoia in 2020 as its first European partner and has backed companies such as Trade Republic, Pennylane, and Rillet. “My conviction on Europe hasn’t moved, and neither am I; when given the opportunity to move to San Francisco, I chose to stay here and focus on this wonderful, imperfect ecosystem.  Europe is where my family is, and where I want to build,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

She further confirmed that she will remain a Sequoia partner, continue serving on portfolio company boards, and also invest personally in the next generation of European founders.

Bek, who spent a decade investing in European founders through Sequoia, backing companies including Revolut, Miro, Attio, and Dust, added that he is already thinking about what the next decade in European venture could look like.

“My heart is in Europe, and I’ve decided to stay here. I’ll continue supporting the founders I work with and serving on my boards,” he said.

The closure of Sequoia’s London office follows a similar move by fellow US VC giant Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), which shuttered its London office in early 2025, less than two years after opening its first international outpost in the UK.

After roughly 20 years of expansion, during which it built multiple businesses across geographies, Sequoia says it is now pulling back to focus on what it does best: high-conviction, highly selective venture capital investing.

As part of this restructuring, the firm has decided to simplify the structure of the Sequoia Capital Fund, sunset its batch accelerator Arc and Scouts programmes, and streamline both its operational and investing teams. It is also eliminating the distinction between its Early and Growth stages, consolidating into one team under a single mission. The firm is also doing away with its Monday partner meeting cycle.

“Founders operate 24/7, and so do we.  Founders shouldn’t have to adhere to our process – we will do our best to adhere to yours,” the firm added.

European founders have already weathered a16z’s exit and now need to prepare for a phase where Sequoia may be hard to reach, especially without a local partner to back them. While the firm has insisted it can keep backing European companies from its Bay Area base, the attention will be on the UK partners who decided to stay, and the European tech ecosystem will watch their next move closely.

]]> FluoRok, an Oxford-based chemical manufacturing startup that has developed a patented process to produce fluorochemicals without using highly hazardous hydrogen fluoride (HF), has secured a €26.64 million ($30 million) Series A financing round.

The round was led by Orano Ventures Fund/Supernova Invest, with participation from investor Bidra Innovation Ventures. Existing backers Oxford Science Enterprises, BGF, GGF, Volta Energy Technologies, and the University of Oxford also participated in the round.

“We back companies whose technologies support a sovereign, sustainable industrial transition. FluoRok has already shown its process works at pilot scale, and taking hydrogen fluoride out of fluorochemical production tackles a safety and supply problem the whole industry shares. We are pleased to join a strong group of investors supporting the team as it moves to industrial scale,” said Florian de Beauchaine, Investment Manager, Orano Venture Fund/Supernova Invest.

FluoRok says its Series A funding round exceeded its original target and included several angel investors, smaller partners such as EverQuest Capital Partners, CPI Enterprises, and WS Investment, as well as approximately €1.15 million ($1.3 million) in grant funding from Innovate UK through its Investor Partnerships programme.

Founded in 2022, FluoRok is a University of Oxford spin-out developing a patented manufacturing platform that bypasses the conventional HF-based process used to produce fluorochemicals entirely. Conventional fluorochemical production has relied on a 250-year-old process that depends on HF, one of the most hazardous chemicals in industrial use, and high-purity fluorspar predominantly sourced from China, creating safety, supply, and cost risks.

FluoRok bypasses this process by relying on mechanical activation combined with base chemistry to unlock fluorine from lower-grade mineral sources and even fluoride-containing industrial waste streams, under controllable conditions. The process runs on off-the-shelf industrial equipment, which makes it faster and easier to scale.

The company targets critical end markets including pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and lithium-ion battery manufacturing, sectors where fluorochemicals are indispensable but supply remains heavily concentrated and hazard-prone.

Dr. Gabriele Pupo, founder and CEO, FluoRok, said, ”We are thrilled to welcome new investors on our journey to fundamentally change how the world makes fluorochemicals, with safer chemistry and better economics.”

“Closing another oversubscribed round, backed by both new and existing investors from around the world, is a testament to the strength of our technology, the incredible commercial traction and the speed of execution of the FluoRok team. This funding will ensure FluoRok can swiftly move from start-up to scale-up and take a further step towards becoming a large-scale industrial manufacturer,” he added.

FluoRok says it has completed pilot qualifications and established strong commercial traction with key customers, with products being validated by more than ten partners across eight countries and three continents.

The Series A funding round builds on the €12.43 million ($14 million) secured in previous rounds and more than €11.54 million ($13 million) in UK and European public funding to date. It plans to use the new capital to transition from startup to industrial scale, including building demonstrator facilities for its reagents and battery electrolyte salts, expanding its team, and deepening its commercial partnerships.

The company also plans to scale its platform for next-generation battery products such as LiFSI and FEC, and for a waste-to-value stream that transforms fluorinated polymer waste, over 25,000 tonnes of which is incinerated annually in Europe alone, into high-value chemical intermediates.

Hera, the European Space Agency’s first mission for planetary defence, arrives at its target body during November, with the goal of gathering precious data on the kinetic impact method of asteroid deflection – while also solving various scientific enigmas.

The small-car-sized spacecraft is headed to the 151-m-diameter Dimorphos asteroid, which orbits in turn around its 780-m Didymos parent. Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022.

DART’s impact caused a brightening visible from distant Earth telescopes, but nobody knows what it did to Dimorphos itself. Hera is going there to perform a close-up crash site survey, to help turn DART’s kinetic impact experiment into a well understood planetary defence deflection technique.

Scientists are hoping for bonus science as well. Past spacecraft close encounters have revealed asteroids to be dynamic environments with complex histories – and many outstanding questions still to be answered. Here are 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore.

]]> Passengers on European flights have faced another morning of security alerts, with a Ryanair flight reportedly targeted by a bomb threat and police investigating threats at Copenhagen Airport and Prague Airport.

The latest incidents follow several days of disruption across Europe, during which passenger planes have been forced to make emergency landings or been diverted due to bomb threats.

Authorities have not established who is behind the threats or whether they are connected.

What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat? What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat?

Ryanair flight from Rome targeted by bomb threat at Lisbon airport

A Ryanair flight arriving at Lisbon’s Humberto Delgado Airport from Rome was reportedly the subject of a bomb threat on Friday morning.

Portugese media reported the service as Flight FR8196. According to reports, Portugal’s Public Security Police (PSP) received an alert about a possible explosive on board the aircraft.

According to Portuguese media, the alert was received through a phone call from a law enforcement officer, rather than an email as in Thursday’s incidents.

The flight arrived at Lisbon on Friday morning.

Copenhagen Airport faces renewed threats as police investigate

Police returned to Copenhagen Airport on Friday after receiving further threats.

Copenhagen police confirmed that officers were present at Denmark’s largest airport while investigations continued.

Copenhagen Airport confirmed the police presence but said flight operations were continuing normally.

It’s not yet clear what threats were made.

Prague Airport investigates renewed threats against passenger aircraft

Bomb threats have also been made against planes at Prague airport, according to Czech police.

Posting on X this morning (6 November), Czech police wrote:

“Today, the threat to place an improvised explosive device on board a number of aircraft arriving at and departing from Prague Airport is being repeated.

“In cooperation with Prague Airport, we have taken the necessary security measures with minimal impact on the airport’s normal operations. We continue to investigate the case.”

Prague Airport has confirmed that airport operations are not affected.

European bomb threats trigger flight diversions and fighter jet escorts

The latest alerts follow extensive disruption across Europe on 5 November, when nearly 30 passenger flights were reportedly targeted by bomb threats. All turned out to be hoaxes.

Airlines affected included Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Finnair, Wizz Air, LOT Polish Airlines and Aegean Airlines.

Several aircraft were diverted, while military fighter jets were deployed to escort passenger flights.

]]> Singapore Airlines has unveiled new first class, business class, premium economy and economy class seats as part of an over S$2 billion (US$1.56 billion) investment in its new long-haul passenger experience. 

The new cabin products will enter service progressively from the second half of 2027 on retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft and the airline’s incoming Boeing 777-9 fleet.

The programme includes 41 A350-900 long-haul and ultra-long-range (ULR) aircraft. The Boeing 777-9 will carry all four new cabin products. The A350 retrofit will introduce redesigned business class seats and, on the A350-900ULR, first class for the first time.

The airline announced the new cabin products, accompanied by a refresh of its inflight entertainment, dining, amenities, connectivity and lounges. 

Singapore Airlines’ new cabin designs draw on research involving more than 5,000 frequent travellers, customers, employees and industry specialists.

New first class seats can form double beds

The new Singapore Airlines first class suites have curved sliding privacy doors. The centre pair can be converted into a two-seat sofa or a double bed measuring 80 inches long and 60 inches wide, which the airline describes as the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Each seat converts into an 80-inch fully flat bed. 

Other features include companion dining, electronically adjustable seating, wireless charging, a 32-inch 4K entertainment screen and controls that can remember a passenger’s preferred seat and lighting settings.

The 777-9 will have six first class seats, while the A350-900ULR will have four.

Business class adds privacy doors and companion beds

Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat features sliding privacy doors, adjustable dividers between centre seats and selected pairs that can be arranged as companion beds.

The fully flat bed measures 79 inches long and up to 24 inches wide. The airline has redesigned the dining table stowage to create more foot space when passengers are lying down. The seats also include adjustable support, wireless charging and entertainment screens of up to 22 inches, depending on aircraft type.

The new business class product will be fitted to both the 777-9 and the retrofitted A350 aircraft.

Collins Aerospace is manufacturing the first class, premium economy and economy seats. RECARO Aircraft Seating will supply business class seats.

Singapore Airlines recruited top industry designers to reimagine its passenger experience. The airline said PriestmanGoode designed the new first class, Designworks designed business class, and Factorydesign designed premium economy and economy class. 

“While each cabin has been designed individually, they are united by the same ambition to make the experience more comfortable, flexible, and rewarding for our customers,” said Lee Lik Hsin, Singapore Airlines’ chief commercial officer.

Premium economy, economy and onboard technology

Singapore Airlines said the premium economy and economy products will offer improvements in comfort, space, convenience and entertainment.

Both classes will feature the next-generation KrisWorld system, with 4K touchscreens and more than 2,500 entertainment options across the new offering.

The system will also support Bluetooth headphone pairing, spatial audio, revised navigation and wellness content. The airline plans Starlink-based high-speed connectivity for its A380 and A350-900 long-haul and ULR aircraft.

Singapore Airlines also announced over 100 new or refreshed dishes and expanded beverage choices across all cabin classes. 

The airline will introduce new amenity kits from November 2026, including SISLEY products in Suites and First Class and BYREDO products in business class. Business class passengers will also receive sleeper suits for the first time.

On the ground, the airline said it has invested more than S$130 million (US$101.5 million) to upgrade and expand its SilverKris lounges.

“This launch marks another major milestone in Singapore Airlines’ unwavering commitment to elevating the end-to-end travel experience,” said Mr Goh Choon Phong, Chief Executive Officer of Singapore Airlines, adding that it was “not an endpoint, but another step in our continuous pursuit to earn and retain the trust and loyalty of our customers, and reinforce our leadership in the airline industry.”

The airline has not yet announced the first routes to receive the new seats. Its latest timetable places the rollout to begin in the second half of 2027.

]]> Boeing uses AI-powered drones to speed up C-17 aircraft inspections https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/boeing-ai-drone-c17-aircraft-inspections/ Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:13:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55888 Boeing is advancing autonomous drone inspections of C-17 Globemaster III aircraft at its San Antonio maintenance facility to detect damage shorten inspections.

The post Boeing uses AI-powered drones to speed up C-17 aircraft inspections appeared first on AGN.

]]> Boeing is testing drone inspections of C-17 Globemaster III transport aircraft at its San Antonio maintenance facility in Texas.

Under its Advanced Aircraft Inspection (AAI) programme, camera-equipped drones fly around the aircraft and photograph its exterior.

Boeing’s Automated Damage Detection Software (ADDS) checks the photographs for possible damage. Technicians then review the findings.

Boeing says the approach could shorten inspections and reduce risky work on elevated platforms.

How Boeing’s drone inspections work

Inspectors normally check the fuselage, wings and other external surfaces from platforms or other access equipment.

The drones photograph areas that would otherwise need close-range inspection. The software flags anything that warrants a closer look. The photographs also give maintenance teams a record they can compare with later inspections.

Boeing is training the software to spot damage such as corrosion and lightning strikes. The software does not make the final assessment. Maintenance staff must examine suspected defects and decide what work is needed.

Boeing says it has tested the main inspection procedures and developed guidance for staff training and quality checks.

Boeing aims to improve aircraft availability

A shorter inspection could return a C-17 to service sooner. The US Air Force and other operators use the C-17 to carry troops, vehicles and equipment, so reducing maintenance downtime is critical.

The drones could also improve worker safety by reducing the need for inspectors to climb onto aircraft or use raised work platforms.

“AAI is about turning innovation into operational value,” said Travis Williams, Boeing vice president of Mobility and Surveillance Aircraft Services. “We’re delivering measurable improvements and building a repeatable capability that can be scaled as we validate outcomes.”

The San Antonio team is still refining the process before wider use.

Drone inspection technology already tested on other military aircraft

The latest announcement follows several years of development involving Boeing and autonomous flight specialist Near Earth Autonomy. Boeing invested in the company through its HorizonX Ventures arm in 2017.

As Defence News reported in 2023, the companies tested autonomous inspections at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam in Hawaii. Early trials proved drones could collect images during inspections and transmit them for automated analysis. Each image is linked to a location on the aircraft so inspectors can check the same area again.

The National Centre for Manufacturing Sciences (NCMS) has also published results from the inspection programme.

NCMS reports that the system cut inspection time by at least 40% during C-17 heavy maintenance visits. The C-17 detection model identified more than 95% of anomalies in each scan. 

The technology has also been tested on other military aircraft, including the KC-46 Pegasus, KC-135 Stratotanker, P-8 Poseidon, EA-18G Growler and C-5 Galaxy.

AI becomes part of Boeing’s wider C-17 maintenance strategy

Boeing is also using aircraft data to help plan C-17 maintenance. In April, the company introduced Aircraft Data Reasoner, software that examines aircraft data for signs of component problems.

“With the Aircraft Data Reasoner, operators gain near‑real‑time insight into component health so we can act before failures occur. That predictive visibility not only improves C-17 mission readiness and reduces unscheduled downtime, but it also drives smarter parts positioning and sustainment decisions across the fleet,” said Williams.

Boeing said an analysis of historical service data indicated a 2%–3% increase in aircraft availability.

In July, Boeing announced plans to work with Pelico on maintenance scheduling and parts supply.

Boeing wants to extend the drone inspection process to other maintenance sites and other aircraft. Its military and commercial maintenance teams are sharing what they learn from the trials.

]]> Ukraine’s F-16 squadron commander “Phantom” says the country’s F-16 fleet has shot down around 4,700 Russian one-way attack drones since entering service.

The total includes the downing of around 1,100 Russian drones in October alone.

Phantom disclosed the figures while speaking at the International Fighter Conference on 5 November.

The figure is understood to exclude interceptions by Ukraine’s limited fleet of ex-French Mirage 2000s and its remaining legacy Soviet fighters.

Phantom cautioned against Ukraine employing too many fighter jet types, suggesting just two: the F-16 and Gripen.

Ukraine is also purchasing the French Rafale, with training expected to start shortly. Its legacy fleet of MiG-29s, Su-24s, Su-27s, and Su-25s is expected to retire once Western jets are available in large enough numbers.

Ukraine F-16s relying on their autocannons to down drones

Phantom said Ukrainian pilots are relying heavily on the cannon as stocks of air-to-air missiles remain constrained.

Ukrainian pilots have previously praised the Mirage’s Matra R.550 Magic (Magic 2) short-range infrared-guided air-to-air missile for use against drones and aerial threats.

F-16s are fitted with a M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel, 20mm rotary Gatling gun, and carry approximately 511 rounds. Among Western fighter jets, this is a large number of rounds.

]]> What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/passenger-aircraft-pilot-bomb-threat Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:10:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55822 From emergency squawk codes to fighter jet escorts, here's how pilots respond when a passenger aircraft receives a bomb threat.

The post What happens when a pilot receives a bomb threat? appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 5 min read
  • Pilots follow security procedures, coordinate with air traffic control and may divert to a nearby airport.
  • Bomb threats can trigger emergency squawk codes, overweight landings and military fighter jet escorts.
  • After landing, passengers may be evacuated while specialist teams inspect the aircraft, baggage and cargo.

A series of bomb threats has forced passenger aircraft to divert across Europe, raising questions about what happens in the cockpit when pilots are warned that an explosive device could be on board.

Flight crews are trained to respond to security emergencies, working with air traffic control, airlines operations teams and specialist authorities to protect passengers and crew.

Depending on the circumstances, the response can involve an aircraft diversion, military assistance and extensive security inspections.

How is a pilot alerted to a bomb threat?

Bomb threats can be received before departure or while an aircraft is airborne. They may be communicated to pilots by their airline’s operating team, or directly through air traffic control.

If a threat is considered sufficiently serious, relevant information is passed to the flight crew, potentially through an aircraft datalink message or air traffic control.

Emma Henderson MBE, former airline captain and aviation expert, told Aerospace Global News: “Our priority is always to keep people safe, so any threat has to be treated seriously every single time.”

What do pilots do when a bomb threat is reported?

Once alerted, the captain and first officer follow their specific airline’s security procedures and checklists.

They would also usually use squawk 7700 to tell air traffic control that there is an emergency. In an “unlawful act of interference”, for example a hijacking or someone taking control of the aircraft, they will likely squawk 7500 instead.

Why might pilots divert rather than continue to their destination?

If the bomb threat is considered credible, the aircraft will normally divert to a suitable airport and land as quickly and safely as possible.

The nearest airport is not always the best option. Pilots will always take into account runway availability, weather, aircraft condition and emergency facilities.

The amount of fuel on board can also affect the decision. An aircraft diverting early on a long-haul flight may still be carrying a lot of fuel, making it heavier than the maximum weight normally allowed for landing. However, if there is a security emergency, the pilots may have to land regardless of the extra weight.

What does squawk 7500 mean? The aviation code no pilot wants to transmit What does squawk 7500 mean? The aviation code no pilot wants to transmit

How does air traffic control handle an aircraft bomb threat?

Air traffic controllers receive specific training for incidents involving potentially explosive devices. They coordinate priority handling, maintain appropriate separation from other aircraft and help organise the diversion.

Controllers are also aware that pilots may be under considerable pressure and managing an increased cockpit workload. Clear communication and coordination with emergency services are therefore essential.

When do fighter jets get involved?

Military fighter aircraft may be scrambled to identify or escort a commercial airliner if additional monitoring is deemed necessary. In the UK, the RAF maintains Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) arrangements, with Typhoon aircraft based at RAF Coningsby and RAF Lossiemouth.

A fighter escort is not automatic and does not mean an explosive device has been confirmed. It is an extra security measure available to military and civilian authorities.

What do cabin crew do during a bomb threat?

Cabin crew look after passengers while following the airline’s security procedures. They communicate with the flight deck, manage the cabin and help passengers remain calm.

If a suspicious item is reported, they follow their training and instructions rather than attempting to investigate or handle it themselves.

How are passenger aircraft designed to reduce the risks of an explosion?

Aircraft manufacturers also evaluate security when designing and building passenger planes.

One example is the Least Risk Bomb Location (LRBL), which is part of certain aircraft safety requirements. It involves considering where an onboard explosion could have the least impact on the aircraft and how important structures and systems can be better protected. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) provides guidance on this in its Advisory Circular AC 25.795-6.

Manufacturers also look at how the aircraft is built and how its cabin pressurisation system works. This system keeps the air pressure inside the cabin at a safe and comfortable level for passengers and crew while flying at high altitudes.

Read: Bomb threats trigger security alerts on seven flights across four European countries Read: Bomb threats trigger security alerts on seven flights across four European countries

What happens to passengers after an emergency aircraft diversion?

After landing, the aircraft will usually be directed to an isolated parking position away from other aircraft and terminal buildings.

Depending on the circumstances, the captain may initiate a Precautionary Rapid Disembarkation, so passengers can leave using mobile steps or stairs rather than emergency slides, which can cause injuries.

If a suspicious item or suspected explosive device is discovered, a more urgent evacuation may be necessary. Specialist teams, potentially including Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) personnel, may inspect the aircraft, baggage and cargo. Further security screening is also likely to be needed before the aircraft can return to service.

“Complacency is never an option”

A bomb threat can disrupt far more than the flight involved. Diversions affect airport schedules, connecting services, aircraft availability and crew planning.

Inspections, crew changes, passenger rebooking and schedule adjustments can have knock-on effects across an airline’s network.

Emma Henderson MBE added:

“From a passenger point of view there is a clear intent to disrupt rather than harm and we can’t bow to the fear that might be creating. We must maintain confidence in air travel while ensuring every warning is taken seriously.”

Crew training, aircraft certification, airport security and cooperation between authorities all contribute to aviation safety.

Another current airline captain we spoke to explained:

“Security and safety are taken extremely seriously by airlines and airports. Flight crews, cabin crews and many airline ground personnel receive regular and thorough security training, keeping them informed on the latest developments and threats within the AVSEC (aviation security) domain and how to deal with them.”

He added: “Ultimately, the objective is to assess every threat, protect passengers and crew, and ensure the necessary security checks are completed before normal operations resume. Even when warnings prove unfounded, complacency is never an option.”
